G1.script: Two hosts on the Guardian bond framework. Host A: This one's honest, which is rare. It basically admits tokenised bonds haven't taken off. Host B: And it says why. The keystone line is "absence of cash on chain" — a bond can't pay its own coupon automatically unless there's tokenised money sitting on the same rails. So the asset side depends entirely on the money side. Host A: Two frameworks, one machine. Host B: Exactly. And here's the quiet part: it says clients still want licensed custodians. So the whole "cut out the middleman" pitch? The middlemen stay — SGX, HSBC, the custodians — and they keep the fees. Host A: So who profits? Host B: The same incumbents, plus whoever owns the data taxonomy, because everyone has to plug into it. Host A: And the citizen? Host B: The citizen's pension is the money underneath these bonds — but the paper never prices what the migration costs, never names who's liable when an automated coupon misfires. The bill lands somewhere; the paper just doesn't say where.
G1.title: G1 · Guardian Fixed Income Framework (2024) — Forensic Analysis

G2.script: Two hosts on the Guardian funds framework. Host A: On the surface this is about making funds cheaper and more accessible. Host B: On the surface. But the real subject is a ladder — mirror, partial, then full on-chain register. And what's climbing that ladder is legal authority. Host A: Meaning who officially owns the record of who owns the fund. Host B: Right, and whoever holds that record holds the fees, the liability, and the veto. It moves from the fund administrator to whoever runs the ledger. Host A: And the framework just doesn't name the administrators it's displacing. Host B: Never. It reads like neutral modernisation. Meanwhile whoever wins the token taxonomy — they call it GCTT — collects a tax off every integration. Host A: What's the cost to an ordinary investor? Host B: Here's the quiet one. "Personalisation" on an immutable ledger means a permanent behavioural record of retail investors. The paper builds the machine and never once discusses privacy. It even admits today's benefits are capped — the real prize needs laws that don't exist yet.
G2.title: G2 · Guardian Funds Framework (2024) — Forensic Analysis

G3.script: Two hosts on Guardian's interlinking paper. Host A: This is the boring-sounding one — how to connect different asset networks together. Host B: Boring until you realise where the danger sits. To move an asset from one network to another, you lock it on one side and mint a copy on the other. That lock-and-mint point is a bridge — and bridges are where the crypto industry has lost the most money, full stop. Host A: And the paper models how bridges work but not how they fail? Host B: Exactly. Who eats the loss when the mint and burn don't match? Silent. Host A: There's also a headline number — four billion a year in savings. Host B: From McKinsey. The same kind of firm that then sells you the transformation project to capture those savings. The interest isn't disclosed. Host A: And the strategy is almost funny. Host B: MAS is running two horses — this pragmatic mesh here, and the grand common platform, GL1, next door. Both funded. The public just doesn't see who's liable when the rails break.
G3.title: G3 · Guardian Interlinking Networks (2023) — Forensic Analysis

G4.script: Two hosts on Bridging the Adoption Gap. Host A: This is Singapore and the UK asking why big investors haven't embraced tokenised assets. Host B: And it's foreworded by Kenneth Gay, the Chief FinTech Officer at Singapore's central bank. His line is "investors at the heart" — technology should serve the investor, not the other way round. Sounds great. Host A: So what's the catch? Host B: The word "investor." All through this paper it means institutions — asset managers, funds. It's written with two industry associations that represent exactly those firms. The ordinary person whose pension is the actual money at the bottom of all this? Not in the room. Host A: So a public official is framing doctrine for a private, institutional build. Host B: And it reads as neutral policy. We're not alleging anything improper — just noting the positioning. Host A: What's missing? Host B: The citizen volume. Nowhere in this whole library does anyone ask whether regular people trust programmable money, or on what terms. The buy-side gets a study. The public gets silence.
G4.title: G4 · Guardian: Bridging the Adoption Gap (2024) — Forensic Analysis

G5.script: Host A: This is the paper where Singapore's wholesale research turns into product. The winning money isn't a central bank digital currency — it's the tokenised bank deposit, the TBL. Host B: And the banks writing the FX standard, OCBC, HSBC, BNY, are the same ones that issue and settle those deposits, and route the flow onto Partior, a consortium rail their own owners sit on. None of that downstream position is disclosed in the paper. Host A: Then there's Ant International — a platform treasury walking in as a client, not an issuer. Co-option by membership. Host B: The catch for the rest of us: whoever drafts the master documentation writes the market, and we don't know who that is. The corporate paying FX fees inherits terms set in a room with no public minutes. Host A: 24/7 settlement also quietly rewrites who bears overnight risk — unpriced. Host B: Neutral-looking plumbing, but the profit and the silence both sit with the standard's own authors.
G5.title: G5 · Guardian FX Workstream (2024) — Forensic Analysis

G6.script: Host A: G6 is the moment tokenised funds stop being a demo. Franklin Templeton, Fidelity, Citi, Deutsche Bank — real logos, real assets. Host B: And Swift, the incumbent everyone said would be disintermediated, shows up holding a bridge workstream. The revolution keeps hiring its own establishment. Host A: The clever part is the enabler stack — KYC and credentialing baked into the rails. Compliance by design. Access is gated before you ever transact. Host B: Two quiet risks. One, a private stablecoin is used to settle a regulated fund before that stablecoin regime is fully licensed — practice outrunning the rules. Two, the paper analyses what happens if a token fails, but not cleanly what happens if the bridge operator itself goes insolvent and sits on your collateral. Host A: For a saver, the surveillance and gatekeeping are engineered in beautifully; the recourse if it breaks is left vague. Host B: Profit is named and logoed. The failure state is where the silence lives.
G6.title: G6 · Operationalising Tokenised Funds (2024) — Forensic Analysis

G7.script: Host A: G7 is Guardian's constitution — it decides not just who can program money, but who is even allowed to exist on the network. That's the trust-anchor idea: banks become the issuers of your digital identity credential. Host B: And look who wrote it. Alan Lim leads for MAS. Among the contributors, from JPMorgan, is Toh Wee Kee — who helped author Singapore's original Ubin project while at MAS. Host A: The same hand on the public research and, years later, on the bank's framework built from it. His affiliation is listed, but nobody flags the revolving door. Host B: The paper even admits public networks reach millions and private ones reach thousands — then builds the private version anyway, without saying what that costs the public. Host A: For an ordinary person, the risk is stark: if a trust anchor drops you, there's no appeal. Your access to tokenised markets is downstream of a bank relationship. Host B: The profit and the identity gatekeeping land with the same institutions whose staff drafted the rules.
G7.title: G7 · Guardian: Open & Interoperable Networks (2023) — Forensic Analysis

P1.script: Two hosts, plain and a little dry. Host A: So this is the founding document — the one every other paper leans on. And the design is two layers: ordinary money underneath, deliberately left dumb, and a smart-contract wrapper on top holding all the conditions. Expiry. Which shops you can spend at. What denominations. Host B: Right, and that split is the whole story, because it means every restriction a citizen ever runs into lives in the wrapper — authored by whoever created the scheme. Expiry isn't physics. It's a field somebody filled in. Host A: Then there's Figure 15, which is the bit that should end an argument. The reference design lets the creator revoke an expired voucher and pull the collateral back. Host B: So when you're told the system can't make an exception — that's a policy choice, not a technical limit. The claw-back path is in MAS's own specification. Host A: And who's in the room? Host B: Eleven entities named in the paper, all of them called neutral things like trial partner. Nearly every one stands to make money if this becomes the standard, and the paper discloses commercial interest for the regulators and almost nobody else. Host A: There's also a quieter one: the separation between the creator and the money-issuer is presented as privacy engineering. Host B: It is — but it's also a pre-built answer to the surveillance-money attack, written years before that attack arrived. Somebody war-gamed the objection early.
P1.title: P1 · PBM Technical Whitepaper (2023) — Forensic Analysis

P10.script: Host A: If you only read one of these, maybe read this one — because this is where the public research quietly becomes a private company. Host B: Project Ubin, final phase, 2020. And look at the author line: it started as eleven banks, and it ends as MAS, Temasek, and JPMorgan. Three names. Host A: And then? Host B: And then, within a year, those same names — JPMorgan, DBS, Temasek — spin up Partior, a private joint venture, selling the exact multi-currency settlement system Ubin just prototyped. Public money proved it; a private firm now owns it. Host A: And the kicker — Partior comes back later as the paid contractor building the BIS Dunbar prototypes. Host B: Public research, private company, public research’s vendor. Twenty-four months. Temasek’s on both sides of that table. Host A: What did citizens get? Host B: Here’s the tell. This wholesale system ships with a "dispute" button built into its escrow messages. The citizen voucher system never got one. The machinery for recourse exists — it was just built for the banks.
P10.title: P10 · Ubin Phase 5 (2020) — Forensic Analysis

P11.script: Host A: On paper this is a rerun. The New York Fed and MAS prove you can settle cross-border FX atomically, under thirty seconds, across different blockchains — using the same lock-and-timeout trick from 2019. Host B: So why do it again? Because the science isn’t the point. The point is the handshake. MAS standing next to the New York Fed says: Singapore is the Fed’s partner on the future of the wholesale dollar. Host A: And there’s a design choice buried in it. Every awkward currency pair gets routed through a "vehicle currency." Host B: Which is the US dollar. So the dollar isn’t just convenient here — it’s wired into the protocol. Dollarisation, wearing a neutrality badge. Host A: Anyone profit from that bridge leg? Host B: Someone has to market-make it and earn the spread — but the experiment literally can’t ask who. It’s out of scope by design. Host A: Citizens? Host B: Nowhere in sight. This is diplomacy conducted by prototype — and the disclaimers are the loudest in the entire library, which tells you exactly how touchy it is.
P11.title: P11 · Cedar II × Ubin+ (2022) — Forensic Analysis

P12.script: Two hosts on Global Layer One. Host A: So Singapore's central bank has a plan for the plumbing of tokenised money, and it calls it "public permissioned." Sounds open. Host B: The word "public" is doing a lot of work. It's open to anyone who meets the criteria — but the criteria are written by the banks running the nodes. Host A: And who's at the table? Host B: BNY, Citi, MUFG, JPMorgan's Onyx, and Société Générale's FORGE. Five global banks helping design a shared ledger they'll then operate — through something called an Operating Company. Host A: Which is basically a company that owns the settlement layer. Host B: Right. The fee and float on trillions in tokenised assets. And nowhere does the paper ask the obvious question: is it fair for a bank-owned utility to set the rules for its own competitors? Host A: Where's the citizen in this? Host B: Nowhere. No buy-side, no ordinary account holder, no public seat. The table is the product, and the public isn't invited to sit at it.
P12.title: P12 · Global Layer One (GL1) Whitepaper (2024) — Forensic Analysis

P13.script: Host A: This is the one where the rulebook stops being a document and becomes part of the wire. Sanctions checks, capital-flow rules — all encoded, and a little cryptographic "proof of compliance" rides along with the payment and releases the funds only if the check passes. Host B: And technically? It’s beautiful. Zero-knowledge proofs, so no raw data ever leaves the bank. Genuinely the best privacy engineering in this whole library. Host A: But privacy for whom? Host B: That’s the whole story. The bank’s data is shielded. The regulator gets real-time monitoring. And the citizen? Nothing. No window into the rules being run on them. Host A: So the same design is privacy for the powerful and a one-way mirror for everyone else. Host B: And nobody in the paper points at the mirror. Meanwhile the commercial rails — Partior, R3’s Corda, SWIFT through an ISO change request — each get validated as "compliant." Everyone at the table wins a lane. Host A: Except the person the money is actually for. Host B: Exactly. The surveillance flows up; the recourse never flows down.
P13.title: P13 · Project Mandala (2024) — Forensic Analysis

P14.script: Host A: Dunbar is the big swing — one shared platform, many central-bank currencies, banks settling directly across borders. And to its credit, it’s brutally honest. Host B: The report basically says: the tech works, that was never the problem. The problem is nobody will put their national money on a platform they don’t control, and there’s no neutral operator everyone trusts. Host A: And who did they hire to build the prototypes? Host B: R3 — and Partior. Which, remember, is the JPMorgan-DBS-Temasek company that came straight out of Singapore’s own Ubin research. So the public project’s private offspring is now the public successor’s paid vendor. Host A: Twenty-four months, full circle. Host B: The revolving door isn’t a person walking through — it’s built into the structure. And the "who operates it" gap Dunbar leaves open becomes the exact business opportunity the next project, GL1, is designed to sell. Host A: Citizens? Host B: Not in the room. This is sovereigns and their vendors deciding who owns the settlement layer — and the honest questions it raises are still unanswered.
P14.title: P14 · Project Dunbar (2022) — Forensic Analysis

P2.script: Two hosts, plain and a little dry. Host A: So this is the paper where Singapore says: we don’t need a digital dollar — but we’re going to build every part of one anyway. Host B: Right, and the giveaway is who’s in the room. Eleven-odd names: DBS, OCBC, UOB doing the tokenised deposits, Grab and Fazz and NETS doing the wallets and the tills, and a government team called OGP running the actual voucher machine. Host A: And they’re all called “trial partners,” very neutral. Host B: Except every one of them makes money if this becomes the standard — and the paper discloses that interest for exactly none of them, only for the regulators. Host A: Here’s the bit that lands on you and me: when you get a CDC voucher today, the shopkeeper waits days or weeks to actually get paid. Somebody earns interest on that money in the meantime. Host B: This new system pays instantly — which sounds great — but nobody says who was quietly pocketing the float before, or where it goes now. Host A: And nobody asks what happens to you when the voucher just expires. Host B: Capability without commitment, they call it. For the citizen it’s conditions without recourse.
P2.title: P2 · Project Orchid Phase 1 (2022) — Forensic Analysis

P3.script: Two hosts, calm and clear. Host A: Okay, this is the boring-looking 2021 paper that actually decides everything. On the surface it says: Singapore doesn’t need a digital dollar, our payments are already cheap and fast. Host B: Fine. But read one layer down and it’s really a document about protecting the banks. Host A: Here’s the number that runs the whole thing — bank deposits are ninety-two percent of the money supply, and those deposits are the banks’ cheap funding. Host B: A really good central-bank digital currency would let people pull money out of banks in a crisis, fast. So the entire design after this is built to make sure any future digital dollar is deliberately unattractive to hold. Host A: Which is clever — but notice who’s being protected, and who isn’t. Host B: The paper models banks, capital flows, stability. It does not model you: which households actually lose out as cash quietly disappears, or whether privacy is a right or just a feature they can switch off. Host A: Those aren’t technical gaps. They’re the questions nobody with a seat at this table was asked to answer.
P3.title: P3 · Retail CBDC: Economic Considerations (2021) — Forensic Analysis

P4.script: Two hosts, wry. Host A: So if the last few papers were about how the money works, this one’s about who gets the keys. The Blueprint sets up two jobs worth a fortune. One: running the official ledger everything settles on. Two — and this is the sneaky one — being “designated” to deploy the smart contracts. Host B: Remember, the smart contract is the wrapper, and the wrapper is where all the rules live. So “who’s allowed to write wrappers” is really “who gets to write the rules of your money.” Host A: And here’s the thing: the paper hands out neither job in public. No tender, no criteria, no expiry date. Host B: But the likely winners are already in the room — BCS, the clearing incumbent, is the obvious ledger operator; and JPMorgan’s Onyx is helping write the very spec it’s positioned to profit from. None of them disclose that interest. Host A: A bank-owned utility writing the rules its competitors have to follow — that’s an antitrust question. Host B: The paper just doesn’t ask it. Host A: The citizen cost isn’t a fee yet. It’s that a public concession is being drawn before anyone gets to object.
P4.title: P4 · Orchid Blueprint (2023) — Forensic Analysis

P5.script: Two hosts, easy pace. Host A: Here’s a funny one. Technically, this 2017 experiment is a shrug — banks park cash with the central bank, get a digital token worth the same, send it to each other. People had done that. Host B: So why does it matter? Host A: Because of the guest list. This is the room where Singapore’s entire digital-money crowd first assembles — the local banks, JPMorgan, the clearing house, the stock exchange, and the consultants writing it all up. Host B: And if you follow the individuals, you see the revolving door before it spins. One man co-writes this as the central bank, and years later signs a related framework as JPMorgan. Another sits in the JPMorgan seat here and goes on to run its blockchain unit — the same unit that later helps write the public money standard its own network then sells into. Host A: And the consultant who authors the report? Host B: Also the party paid to make it look like a success. Host A: None of that is a scandal by itself. Host B: But it means the official story of what worked was written by the people who stood to profit from it. Worth remembering when a later paper says the technology led them here.
P5.title: P5 · Ubin Phase 1 (2017) — Forensic Analysis

P6.script: Two hosts, understated. Host A: This is the one that quietly embarrasses everything that came after it. In 2017, MAS and the banks build a prototype settlement system with no central operator — the machine runs itself, privately, across three different platforms. Host B: And the report actually says out loud: maybe MAS doesn’t need to be the operator anymore. Feasible. Proven. On the record. Host A: Then what happens? Host B: Six years later the official Blueprint puts the operator firmly back in the middle, permissioned, gated, incumbents keeping their seats. Host A: So when someone tells you the closed design was forced by the technology — this document is the receipt that says otherwise. Host B: And notice who ran the study: the central bank, yes, but co-led by the banks’ own association, and written up by a consultant paid to deliver it. Host A: A decentralised system would have quietly deleted a fee-and-oversight structure those same players sit on. Host B: Nobody writes that sentence down. But it’s the most honest explanation for why the road that worked was the road not taken.
P6.title: P6 · Ubin Phase 2: Re-imagining RTGS (2017) — Forensic Analysis

P7.script: Two hosts, pointed but calm. Host A: Here’s the detail that should bother you. In 2018, MAS and the stock exchange build a settlement system for banks trading government bonds. And look at what they carefully build in: multi-signature controls, time limits, a way to recover assets, and — this is the key word — arbitration. Host B: If a trade goes wrong, there’s a dispute state, a reversal state, a path to appeal. Host A: Now hold that next to the system built for ordinary people, the purpose-bound voucher. That one has one ending: expired. No dispute, no appeal, no reversal. Host B: The exact machinery the banks got, the citizens didn’t. And MAS already owns it — they designed it here — they just never reused it for the public. Host A: Why? Host B: Follow the table. The bank side is co-chaired by the exchange that profits from the settlement business, and its recourse protects institutional money. The citizen side had no one at the table whose revenue depended on giving people a way to complain. Host A: Same architecture, opposite recourse. Host B: That’s not a technical limitation. That’s a decision about who is worth protecting.
P7.title: P7 · Ubin Phase 3: DvP on DLT (2018) — Forensic Analysis

P8.script: Host A: So this is 2019 — the first time anyone settles two different central-bank currencies atomically, across two different blockchains, no middleman. Canadian dollars on Corda, Singapore dollars on Quorum. Host B: Right, and the headline is "we removed the trusted third party." Except read the fine print — they didn’t remove trust, they relocated it. Into code, and into a timeout parameter someone has to set by hand. Host A: Bank of Canada and MAS are the public authors. But look who’s in the room building it — J.P. Morgan, who wrote the Quorum leg, and Accenture on integration. Host B: And that’s the pattern. J.P. Morgan shows up again at Ubin Phase 5, then again through Partior, selling the multi-currency rails this experiment prototyped. Public research, private vendor, no disclosure. Host A: What about the citizen? Host B: They’re not in this one at all — it’s wholesale. But the habit starts here: the public pays for the proof, and a private firm keeps the product.
P8.title: P8 · Jasper–Ubin Design Paper (2019) — Forensic Analysis

P9.script: Host A: This one’s the origin story — before any of the fancy blockchain demos, somebody had to write down why cross-border payments are broken. Three central banks, 2019. Host B: And the number that matters: flows heading to thirty trillion dollars a year, but the number of correspondent banks carrying them fell eight percent. More money, fewer pipes. Host A: Which is a concentration-risk story. But here it gets re-branded as an innovation opportunity. Host B: And notice who holds the pen on the commercial side — HSBC. The biggest correspondent bank on earth, helping describe the "future state." Plus OCBC, TD, UOB, and KPMG facilitating. Host A: So the incumbents got to shape what the replacement looks like. Host B: Exactly — and the two safe, incremental options are the ones that got real money. The genuinely radical idea, a basket-backed wholesale CBDC, gets parked on paper and never owned. Host A: Citizen angle? Host B: Invisible again. This is a wholesale conversation about who clears whose money — households never enter the frame, and won’t for the rest of the corpus.
P9.title: P9 · Cross-Border Interbank Payments (2019) — Forensic Analysis

X1.script: Host A: This is where the whole story starts — nine pages, October 2008, six weeks after Lehman. A pseudonymous author, Satoshi, proves money can move without banks. Host B: And the money trail is strange because there isn't one. No sponsor, and a fortune of about a million coins that's never been touched. Host A: There's a Tier-3 question we keep open, never assert: could this have come from the same establishment the rest of the library documents — a controlled test? The timing is surgical, the crypto is NSA-grade SHA-256. Host B: But against that, there's a 25-year cypherpunk lineage — Chaum, Back, Dai, Szabo — and a genesis message mocking the bailout. So we hold it as a question. Host A: What's not a question is what happened next. Officials kept the ledger and stripped everything that made it free — permissionless became licensed, irreversible became revocable. Host B: Bitcoin tested on volunteers who opted in. The voucher stack tests expiry and revocation on a whole population that never did — and isn't shown the clock.
X1.title: X1 · Satoshi — Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (2008) — Forensic Analysis

X2.script: Host A: March 2018, the BIS publishes the first official CBDC framework. It sounds dry — a taxonomy, wholesale versus general-purpose. But that split becomes the literal org chart of Singapore's decade of work. Host B: What's striking is who's in the room. One chair is Benoît Cœuré, who resurfaces in 2020 signing the global principles and running the BIS Innovation Hub. The other is Jacqueline Loh — Deputy Managing Director of Singapore's own central bank. Host A: So while MAS is two years into its Ubin pilots, a MAS deputy is co-writing the world's CBDC doctrine. The “global” lane and the “Singapore” lane aren't parallel — they share people. Host B: The document also warns your bank deposits could flee to the central bank, and builds the whole system to protect the banks first. Host A: And the one party never mentioned is you — the citizen. No consent, no programmability question. Host B: “No decision to issue” became the cover to build everything anyway.
X2.title: X2 · BIS CPMI — Central Bank Digital Currencies (2018) — Forensic Analysis

X3.script: Host A: November 2018, Singapore Fintech Festival. Christine Lagarde, head of the IMF, stands up and says we should consider issuing digital currency. Eight months earlier the BIS had said “go slow.” Now the world's top monetary official says go. Host B: And the stage matters. She says it at MAS's own festival, two years into Singapore's pilots. The venue crowns Singapore as the lab. Host A: Follow the person, not just the institution. In 2020, as head of the European Central Bank, Lagarde chairs the group that signs the global principles. One person carries the arc from question to answer. Host B: She sells it on privacy and inclusion — protection from data-hungry platforms. But trace where the privacy engineering actually landed: on the banks' wholesale rails. Host A: The citizen got the vocabulary — inclusion, safety, privacy. The institutions got the engineering. Host B: And the retail user got a lifecycle that ends at “Expired,” with no way to appeal.
X3.title: X3 · IMF Lagarde — Winds of Change (2018) — Forensic Analysis

X4.script: Host A: October 2020 is the hinge. Seven central banks plus the BIS publish shared principles for digital currency. After this, the question stops being “should we” and becomes “how do we build it.” Host B: And the signatures are familiar. Cœuré, from the 2018 BIS paper, co-chairs. Lagarde, who made the case in Singapore in 2018, now chairs the governors' group as head of the ECB. Same small cast, bigger mandates. Host A: The key clause is quiet: “an appropriate role for the private sector.” That's the banks' insurance — whatever gets built arrives through them, not around them. Host B: And the timing is the punchline. Singapore's voucher scheme was already live in 2020, before the ink dried. The doctrine was catching up to Singapore, not the other way round. Host A: Grade the real product against these principles: cash coexistence — vouchers are app-only. Do no harm — 44% breakage. Clear legal framework — no accounting for expired value, no appeal. Host B: The yardstick is theirs. The failing marks are ours to notice.
X4.title: X4 · BIS — CBDC Foundational Principles (2020) — Forensic Analysis
